opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that the projects in the ACM class are very hands-on, and they force you to build real systems end to end. You're not just learning concepts from a textbook. You're asked to write a compiler, build a simple CPU, implement parts of an operating system, things like that. When you take on something at that scale as an undergraduate, you quickly realize that understanding an idea and actually making it work are two very different things.

Those projects teach you how all the layers fit together. When you write a compiler and then run its output on hardware you designed yourself, you start to see the whole stack, from the high-level language down to the machine. That full-stack view stayed with me. A lot of what I did later, like XGBoost, TVM, and machine learning systems in general, comes from that same instinct: don't treat any layer as a black box, and be willing to go down and touch the lower levels when you need to.

There's also a training in persistence and debugging. These projects are big. Things break in ways you don't expect, and nobody hands you the answer. You have to read code, reason carefully, and sometimes stay up late tracking down one bug. That builds a kind of engineering muscle and a confidence that if you sit with a hard problem long enough, you can work it out.

And it's a community. Everyone around you is doing the same hard projects, so you learn a lot from your classmates and the senior students who TA'd. That culture, where building things is normal and expected, really shaped how I think about research. For me, good research often starts with actually building something that works and that other people can use.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think back on the ACM class at Shanghai Jiao Tong, the course projects are honestly the part that shaped me the most. The reason they worked so well is that they weren't toy assignments. You were asked to build real systems from the ground up: a compiler, a CPU, a database. Not a module of one, the whole thing, end to end.

That changes how you learn. When you only solve isolated problems, you never experience how the pieces fit together or where the real difficulty hides. Building a complete system forces you to confront everything at once. You design the architecture, you make tradeoffs, you hit bugs that cross layers, and you have to live with your earlier decisions. There is nowhere to hide. If the design is wrong, you find out weeks later when everything stops working, and you learn why it was wrong in a way no lecture can teach you.

The second thing is the time scale. These projects ran for a semester, sometimes longer. You had to plan, manage your own schedule, and keep going when things were broken for days. That taught persistence and engineering discipline. Research is very similar. Most of the time things don't work, and the skill is pushing through with a clear mind.

And third, there was a strong peer culture. Everyone was building the same ambitious thing, so you were constantly comparing approaches, debugging together, and being pushed by people who were very good. That kind of environment raises your sense of what is possible.

I think a lot of what I did later, with XGBoost, with TVM, with MXNet, came from that habit of saying, let me just build the whole system and see what happens. The ACM projects gave me the confidence that a small team, or even one person, can build something complete and real. That confidence is probably the most valuable thing I took from it.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that a course project asks you to go beyond understanding an idea—you actually have to make it work. In a lecture, the problem is usually well defined. In a project, you have to decide how to approach it, implement something, and figure out why the result is different from what you expected. That process connects theory with practice.

And when your classmates are working on projects too, you learn from their approaches. Someone makes a different design choice, and that pushes you to think about your own. So you’re practicing more than programming: you’re learning how to explore an open-ended problem, make tradeoffs, and explain what you’ve built. Those skills carry over very naturally into research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most valuable part is that you have to turn an idea into something that actually works. In a typical course, the problem is already defined, and there is usually a known answer. In a course project, you have to decide what problem to solve, understand what has already been done, and figure out how to evaluate your solution. And often your first idea doesn’t work, so you have to understand why and try again.

That process brings together a lot of skills: reading papers, implementing systems, running experiments, and communicating the results. It also gives students room to take ownership. You’re not just learning a technique because it will be on an exam; you’re learning it because you need it to build something you care about. I think that’s very good preparation for research.
